Lesson 01

Fine-tune only after a measured failure of the cheaper fixes

Why it matters

Prompt, schema, retrieval, and tools come first. Training is for a gap those did not close.

Try it: Prompt, retrieval, or fine-tune

Lesson
01 of 05
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Order
Prompt, schema, retrieval, tools
Train
Only for the leftover gap
Still
Compare to the base

Fine-tuning changes the model's weights, usually by training on examples of the behavior you want. It costs data work, compute, and a new model you have to host and re-eval. It is the right tool when the base model already has the facts — or you will keep retrieving the facts — and still will not hold a format, a style, or a domain decision that you can show in examples.

Do not fine-tune to

  • Memorize a handbook that changes monthly. Retrieve it.
  • Hide a secret or a policy the prompt already states and the eval already passes.
  • Repair a broken tool. Fix the tool.
  • Chase a leaderboard with no task of your own.

The decision record is the eval from School 09 plus a sentence: which failures remain, and why a prompt or a retrieval change cannot address them. If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to train.

Practice

Write that decision sentence for a real or fictional system. 'Not yet, because …' is a complete answer.

Check

Name one problem retrieval solves better than fine-tuning.

Show the answer

Facts that change, or facts that must be cited from a source you can update without training.

Lesson 02

LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen

Why it matters

QLoRA does the same while the frozen base is stored in a quantized form.

Try it: LoRA rank

Lesson
02 of 05
Time
13 min
Level
Core
Train
Small matrices
Freeze
The base
QLoRA
Quantized base, same adapter idea

Full fine-tuning updates every weight. That is expensive and easy to damage. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the base model and trains small matrices that sit alongside certain layers. You store the adapter, not a full second copy of the model. At inference you load the base plus the adapter.

QLoRA quantizes that frozen base so the training job fits on a smaller GPU. The adapter is still what you train. People say 'I quantized' when they mean 'I fine-tuned' and the reverse. In a design review, say which one you did.

Preference methods such as DPO train from pairs of better and worse answers. They are a fit when the issue is which output a person prefers, and a poor fit when the issue is a missing document. You still need a base that can produce the better answer often enough to learn from.

Tools you will see named

Hugging Face PEFT, Axolotl, Unsloth, and the hosted fine-tuning APIs from the major labs. The method matters more than the brand: frozen base, small adapter, same eval before and after.

Practice

In three sentences, explain to a teammate the difference between quantizing a model to run it and training a LoRA adapter on it.

Check

What do you save after a LoRA run?

Show the answer

The adapter, and a record of the base model id it attaches to. The adapter without the matching base is not a model.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Loss sketch

A sketch of a shape you will see in training write-ups. Training loss falls. Validation loss can rise when the run memorizes. This is not a log from a named model.

Lesson 03

Training data has a format, a license, and a leakage problem

Why it matters

Examples teach the behavior. They also teach secrets you forgot were in the log.

Try it: Prompt, retrieval, or fine-tune

Lesson
03 of 05
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Examples
Teach the behavior
Also teach
Secrets left in the log
Split
Train is not the test

A typical supervised set is a list of conversations or instruction pairs: the input the model will see, and the output you want. The format must match how you will call the model later. Training on essays and then calling the model as a JSON API is a self-inflicted miss.

  • You need the right to train on every row. A model license, a website's terms, and your employer's policy can each forbid it.
  • Remove secrets, tokens, and personal data. A model that memorizes a key is a leak you cannot easily grep.
  • Remove exact copies of your eval tasks. If the eval is in the training set, the score is a memory test.
  • Include refusal and 'not in the source' examples if that is the behavior you want. A set of only happy paths teaches invention.
  • Keep a validation split that you do not train on.

Synthetic data

Data a model wrote is allowed only if you review it and you are allowed to use it. It repeats the teacher's mistakes at scale. A person still owns the guidelines.

Practice

Describe the columns of a training row for one task. Add a column for the source of the row and a yes/no for 'contains personal data'. That yes/no must be no before the row is usable.

Check

Why must eval tasks stay out of the training set?

Show the answer

Because a high score would then mean the model saw the answers, not that it generalized.

Lesson 04

Compare the adapter to the base model on the same tasks

Why it matters

Keep the adapter only if the scorecard says so, including the tasks that used to pass.

Try it: LoRA rank

Lesson
04 of 05
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Same
Tasks and grader
Count
Regressions
Keep
Only if the card says so

Run the School 09 tasks twice: base model, then base plus adapter. Same prompts, same retrieval, same tools. The adapter wins only if the failures you trained for improved and the safety tasks did not get worse.

Watch for a model that learned the training phrasing and now refuses to answer a valid variant. That shows up as regressions on tasks that used to pass. It is the usual cost of a small, narrow set.

  • Record the base id and the adapter id together.
  • If you quantize after training, eval the quantized result, not the pre-quantized one you will not ship.
  • If the adapter ties the base, do not ship it. You would be adding an artifact to host for no gain.

Practice

Write the comparison header: task, base result, adapter result, regression yes/no. Fill it with the decision you expect, and note which safety task would make you throw the adapter away.

Check

A adapter raises the average and fails a refusal task the base passed. Do you ship it?

Show the answer

No, if refusal is in the gate. An average can rise while a safety regression lands.

Lesson 05

Prefer a prompt or a tool when that is the whole gap

Why it matters

Most 'we should fine-tune' reviews end with a schema, a retrieval fix, or a smaller model.

Try it: Prompt, retrieval, or fine-tune

Lesson
05 of 05
Time
8 min
Level
Practice
Usual end
Schema, retrieval, or a smaller model
Train for
A pattern the index will not hold
Do not train
Facts you can update

Walk this list before you spend on training.

  1. The output shape is underspecified. Fix the schema.
  2. The fact is missing from the context. Fix retrieval or the tool.
  3. The fact is in the context and ignored. Fix placement, chunking, or the instruction to cite.
  4. A cheaper model fails and a larger base model passes. Use the larger model, or route only the hard rows.
  5. Only the remaining rows, with a stable behavior you can exemplify, are training candidates.

This is the judgment hiring panels are probing when they ask 'how do you decide to fine-tune'. The answer is a sequence of measured exclusions, not enthusiasm for training.

Practice

Take the decision sentence from 10-01 and run it down this list. Stop at the first item that applies.

Check

When is a larger base model a better answer than a fine-tune?

Show the answer

When the larger model already passes the same tasks and you can afford it. You have not found a behavior the base cannot learn from context.
